Proceed as follows:
1. Prepare the concentrations of vitamin C solution as decided in (a)(i) and Fig. 1.1.
You are required to find the volume of DCPIP needed to reach the end-point for each of the
concentrations of vitamin C solution prepared in (a)(i).
2. Put 3 cm of the lowest concentration of vitamin C solution into a test-tube.
3. Put 5 cm of DCPIP into the syringe, labelled D.
4. Wipe off any drops of DCPIP from the outside of the syringe with a paper towel.
5. Hold the syringe over the test-tube and push the plunger gently to release one or two drops of
DCPIP as shown in Fig. 1.2.

6. Shake the test-tube to mix the contents.
7. Repeat step 5 and step 6 until the blue colour remains (does not disappear). This is the
end-point.
8. Record in (a)(ii) the volume of DCPIP needed to reach the end-point.
If the colour does not remain blue after adding 5 cm of DCPIP, stop putting in DCPIP and
record as ‘more than 5’.
9. Repeat step 2 to step 8 for each of the concentrations of vitamin C solution that you prepared
in step 1.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Vitamin C is important in the human diet. It is essential for the growth and repair of tissues in
the body.
Some vegetables contain vitamin C and can be eaten either uncooked (raw) or cooked.
A scientist carried out an investigation to determine the effect of heating on the vitamin C
content of selected vegetables. The scientist measured the vitamin C content in 100 g of each
food sample when raw and after boiling for 10 minutes.
All other variables were kept constant.
The results are shown in Table 1.1.
Table 1.1
vitamin C content

broccoli (B) 79 44

parts.text:
Plot a chart of the data shown in Table 1.1.
Each pair of bars should be separated for each type of vegetable.

You may lose marks if you do not show your working.

In raw vegetables vitamin C is contained within the cells of the tissues.
Suggest how boiling causes the loss of vitamin C in broccoli.
